svg.aria-label: How to write ஆம்: 3 parts, ஆ, ம, ், one after another
svg.title: Writing ஆம்
svg.desc: 3 parts written one after another: ஆ, ம, ் (tamil). The parts are in the order the hand writes them, which is not always the order they are typed: a vowel sign written to the left of its consonant comes before it. Each vowel sign is drawn on its own, without the consonant it attaches to. Each part has its own group of frames; frame N of a group shows movements 1 to N of that part, the movement being added drawn in ink over the finished part, whose outline is read from _fonts/NotoSansTamil-Static.ttf. Each part is drawn at its own scale from its own cited stroke order, so the strip does not show how large the parts are next to each other, how far apart they sit, or any join between them. Stroke order: ஆ: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 4, ஆ (Univ. of Texas at Austin), p. 192; drawn in one stroke after HP Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Tamil recognizer, class 1 (ஆ): stored online-handwriting prototypes from native writers (MIT licence, 2012) <https://sites.la.utexas.edu/tamilscript/files/2009/08/hw_lettersinstructions.pdf>; ம: Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 1 (Univ. of Texas at Austin) <https://sites.la.utexas.edu/tamilscript/files/2009/08/hw_lettersinstructions.pdf>; ்: Abhinaya Rajarajan, Varai (Swift Student Challenge 2026), reference drawings recorded by hand for the 18 Tamil consonants with pulli, க் to ன் (repository commit 952294fa, no licence: facts only) <https://github.com/abhinayaRajarajan/varai>. Source notes on variation: ஆ: Appendix I Frame 4 numbers ஆ's movements and gives the right upright a number of its own after the horizontal; this ductus used to read that as a pen lift, but a numbered movement is not evidence of one. In HP Labs India's online Tamil handwriting data (the LipiTk 4.0 Tamil isolated-character recognizer, trained on hpl-tamil-iso-char), 28 of the 29 stored prototypes of ஆ (97%) are one pen-down stroke. All 28 start in the upper half, at the curl. In 26 of them (93%) the pen runs on from the horizontal up the right upright to its top and then comes back down it, and 21 (75%) end at the bottom right, in the long-vowel loop. So this ductus overrides the old lift: it follows Frame 4's movements in order without lifting, climbs the upright from the end of the horizontal, draws it down over that ink and runs on into the loop. The traces are scaled to a square, so they fix the stroke count, the start, the order and the direction, not the proportions: the path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Tamil outline. The underlying HP Labs data is licensed for research use only, so only counts and shares are cited here, and no trace was copied. Tamil handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation; there is no single national stroke-order standard. ம: Tamil handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation; there is no single national stroke-order standard. This is one attested order. ்: One writer's recorded reference drawings, stored in the order they were drawn. In all 18 the consonant body is one stroke and the puḷḷi is a separate second stroke, made after the body is complete, so it costs one pen lift. Its centre sits above the body at 0.47 to 0.65 of the body's width (0.54 for க்). An earlier reading of Info-farmer's Writing Tamil animations of the consonants on Wikimedia Commons, which show each consonant with its puḷḷi, also places the dot after the body. Confidence is medium: one recorded writer, and only stroke count, order and the dot's bounding box were read; the dot is about 10 by 13 canvas units, too small to say which way the pen moved, so the short downward dab drawn here is not a claim. The path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Tamil disc, which the font centres at 0.43 to 0.60 of the consonant's width, a little left of where this writer put it. Handwriting varies by writer.
svg.text: How it is written — 3 parts, one after another
Part 1 of 3 — one unbroken stroke · 7 movements
Part 2 of 3 — one unbroken stroke · 5 movements
Part 1: stroke order after Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 4, ஆ (Univ. of Texas at Austin), p. 192; drawn in one stroke after HP
Labs India, Lipi Toolkit, Lipi Indic Character Recognizers 4.0, Tamil recognizer, class 1 (ஆ): stored online-handwriting prototypes from native writers (MIT licence, 2012)
Part 2: stroke order after Sankaran Radhakrishnan, Tamil Script Learners Manual, Appendix I: Hand-movements, Frame 1 (Univ. of Texas at Austin)
Part 3: stroke order after Abhinaya Rajarajan, Varai (Swift Student Challenge 2026), reference drawings recorded by hand for the 18 Tamil consonants with pulli, க் to ன் (repository
This order is attested, not standardised; the source records where it varies.
